name: West Virginia
note: In West Virginia the funeral director or other person who takes custody of the body collects the personal data, including the social security number. They send the certificate within 48 hours to the physician, physician assistant or APRN, who certifies the cause within 24 hours of receiving it. The certificate is then filed with the Section of Vital Statistics within five days of death and before final disposition. The certifier files the electronic cause of death when filing is electronic. Reportable deaths go to the Office of the Chief Medical Examiner or the county medical examiner, who certifies within 48 hours, and every cremation needs a medical examiner's or coroner's authorization. From registration, local registrars send monthly copies to the county clerk, who keeps a public register of deaths. The clerk cancels voter registrations on the registrar's death certificate or a Secretary of State records match, and the State Registrar may furnish data to government agencies and national statistics. Certified copies are limited to close family, legal guardians, their representatives and people protecting a personal or property right.

steps.title: Pronounce death in an institution
steps.who: The certifying practitioner or another physician. If none is available, a designated licensed health professional who views the body.
steps.summary: With the certifier's permission, the health professional who pronounces may release the body to the funeral director. Deaths during court-ordered hospitalisation, in a correctional facility or in police custody must go straight to a medical examiner or coroner. Otherwise the place where death is pronounced counts as the place of death.

steps.title: Report reportable deaths to the medical examiner
steps.who: The attending physician. If none, a law-enforcement officer who knows of the death, the funeral director or any other person present.
steps.trigger: Death by violence or apparent suicide, sudden death in apparent good health, an unattended death, death of an inmate of a public institution, a public-health threat, or a suspicious, unusual or unnatural death.
steps.summary: A physician, officer, funeral director or embalmer who wilfully fails to notify commits a misdemeanour (fine of $100–$500). The chief or county medical examiner takes charge of the body.

steps.title: Medical examiner certifies investigated deaths
steps.who: The state Medical Examiner or designee, the county medical examiner or the county coroner where the death occurred or the body was found.
steps.trigger: A death requiring inquiry under chapter 61, article 12.

deadline.text: within forty-eight hours after taking charge of the case

steps.summary: If the cause is not known, 'Pending' is entered and amended later, and supplemental reports go to vital statistics. A medical examiner who declines jurisdiction may direct the family physician or the pronouncing physician to certify.

steps.title: Funeral director sends the certificate to the certifier
steps.who: The funeral director or other person who takes custody of the body. They get the personal data, including the decedent's social security number, from the next of kin or the best qualified source.
steps.summary: The funeral director starts the certificate and passes it to the practitioner who will complete the medical certification.

steps.title: Complete the medical certification
steps.who: The physician, physician assistant or APRN in charge of the patient's care for the fatal condition. Failing them, an associate or covering physician, the institution's chief medical officer, or the physician who did an autopsy.
steps.trigger: Receipt of the certificate from the funeral director.

deadline.text: within twenty-four hours after receipt of the certificate of death

steps.summary: The certifier attests by signature or an approved electronic process. Under electronic filing, the certifier files the electronic cause-of-death certification directly. Final disposition waits until the certifier authorises it if the cause is delayed.

steps.title: File the death certificate with the Section of Vital Statistics
steps.who: The funeral director or other person who assumed custody of the body, once the medical certification is received.

deadline.text: within five days after death, and prior to final disposition

steps.summary: The certificate is filed with the Section of Vital Statistics, or as the State Registrar directs (for example, through a local registrar). Wilfully violating the article or refusing a duty is a misdemeanour, punishable by up to $1,000 or a year in jail.

steps.title: Local registrar transmits certificates to the State Registrar
steps.who: Local and deputy local registrars appointed by the State Registrar.
steps.summary: Certificates go by mail or an approved electronic process, on the State Registrar's schedule.

steps.title: Authorization for final disposition; cremation needs a medical examiner
steps.who: The physician or the state or county medical examiner authorises disposition. For cremation, the state Medical Examiner, county medical examiner or county coroner.
steps.trigger: Intended burial, cremation or other final disposition.
steps.summary: No sexton may allow an interment without the authorization. Cemeteries return authorizations within ten days of disposition, and the funeral director sends all of a month's authorizations to the State Registrar by the tenth of the next month. Moving a body without a permit is a misdemeanour.

steps.title: Monthly lists from institutions and funeral directors
steps.who: The administrator of each institution (deaths that occurred there) and each funeral director (bodies prepared or disposed of).

deadline.text: not later than the tenth day of the following month

steps.summary: These monthly lists give the Section of Vital Statistics a cross-check against certificates actually filed.

steps.title: Certified copies to close family and those with a right to protect
steps.who: The registrant's parents, spouse, adult children, grandchildren or great-grandchildren, legal guardian, or their authorised representative. Others who show the record is needed to determine or protect a personal or property right.
steps.summary: Issued by the State Registrar and other authorised custodians. Copying vital records otherwise is unlawful, and death records become public 50 years after the death.

steps.title: Monthly death certificate copies to the county clerk
steps.who: The local registrar, to the county clerk of the county of death. The State Registrar also sends a copy to the clerk of the county where the decedent lived, if different.
steps.summary: From these copies the county clerk, who is also the voter registration official, compiles a register of deaths.

steps.title: County clerk cancels deceased voters' registrations
steps.who: The clerk of the county commission, on a death certificate from the Registrar of Vital Statistics, a Secretary of State records match, an obituary, or a family affidavit. The Secretary of State coordinates the statewide database with state agency records.
steps.trigger: Notice of death from these sources.
steps.summary: Cancellation is mandatory once the death is verified. No state agency may withhold a voter's deceased status from the Secretary of State without a court order.

steps.title: Data to national vital statistics
steps.who: The State Registrar, under an agreement with the federal agency responsible for national vital statistics.
steps.summary: The department must enter into an agreement setting the statistical or research uses and the federal support.

steps.title: Records and data to government agencies; birth-death matching
steps.who: Federal, state and local government agencies for their official duties; other states' vital records offices by agreement.
steps.trigger: An agency request or agreement; registration of a death.
steps.summary: The State Registrar may furnish copies or data to agencies for official duties. To prevent fraud, it may post the fact of death to the birth certificate, and copies of such birth certificates are marked 'deceased'.

steps.title: Private bodies rely on certified copies
steps.who: The family or personal representative presents a certified copy. Others may apply only by showing a personal or property right.
steps.summary: No West Virginia statute read here gives banks or insurers a data route to vital records. Private verification runs through the federal layer (LADMF).

steps.title: County register of deaths is a public record
steps.trigger: Monthly receipt of death certificate copies.
steps.summary: The clerk's register of deaths, compiled in a form the State Registrar prescribes, is open to the public. The certificates themselves stay confidential.

steps.title: Published notice of administration of the estate
steps.who: The clerk of the county commission (the probate body).
steps.trigger: Filing of the estate appraisement, or 120 days after the personal representative qualifies if none is filed.

deadline.text: within thirty days of the filing of the appraisement

steps.summary: The notice names the decedent and personal representative and runs weekly for two weeks as a legal advertisement. Claims must be filed within sixty days of first publication.

registrationDeadlineDays.note: Within five days after death and before final disposition.

informantDuty.note: The funeral director or other person who takes custody of the body files; next of kin supply the personal data.

medicalExaminerScrutiny.note: No review of every certificate, but every cremation needs authorization from the state or county medical examiner or the county coroner.

electronicRegistration.note: The statute provides for electronic filing of the cause of death by the certifier and electronic transmission by local registrars, 'as directed by the State Registrar and in accordance with legislative rule'. It does not mandate electronic filing for all.

centralPopulationRegister.note: No population register; the Section of Vital Statistics holds the death record, with county clerks keeping a public register of deaths.

governmentPropagation.note: Under state law, registration reaches the county clerk monthly, which feeds both the public death register and mandatory voter cancellation, with a statewide database matched by the Secretary of State. Other agencies only on request. No state provision found reaches the DMV, Medicaid or the State Tax Department. Federal feeds (SSA) are in the us-federal layer.

certificateAccess.note: Parents, spouse, adult children, grandchildren, great-grandchildren, legal guardian or representatives, and others with a personal or property right. The county register of deaths is public, and records open 50 years after death.

gaps: Pointer § 3-2-19 concerns municipal election records, not deaths. The death provisions are §§ 3-2-23 and 3-2-4a (and § 3-2-21(i)), cited instead.

The legislative rule on vital statistics (the 64 CSR series on electronic death filing and on who else may obtain copies) was not read; apps.sos.wv.gov was not tried. So the scope of mandatory electronic filing is not established.
W. Va. Code chapter 16 article 5 was enumerated by probing §§ 16-5-1 to 16-5-45 (16-5-39 onward do not exist). The site search was not used, per the DER note that it always returns 0.
No state statute was found sending deaths to the Division of Motor Vehicles, WV Medicaid or the State Tax Department. Chapters 17B, 9 and 11 were not searched.
No West Virginia provision read here mentions an electronic death feed to SSA. It is left to the us-federal layer.
privateSectorVerification is left to the us-federal layer (LADMF). West Virginia law gives private bodies no vital records route beyond applying for a copy on a property-right basis.
